title: Finiteness of upper bounded integrable rational weight modules
statement: Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional split semisimple Lie algebra over $\mathbf Q$ [def-wf-lie-algebra, def-wf-semisimple-lie-algebra], with splitting maximal abelian subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, roots $R$, coroots $h_\alpha$ and simple-root base $\Delta=\{\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r\}$ as in [lem-sfb-split-semisimple-root-decomposition]. Choose nonzero $e_i\in\mathfrak g_{\alpha_i}$ and $f_i\in\mathfrak g_{-\alpha_i}$ with $[e_i,f_i]=h_{\alpha_i}$. Let $M$ be any rational representation of $\mathfrak g$, not assumed finite-dimensional or cyclic, having an ordinary weight decomposition $$M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in\mathfrak h^\vee}M_\mu,\qquad M_\mu=\{v:hv=\mu(h)v\ \forall h\in\mathfrak h\},$$ with every $M_\mu$ finite-dimensional. Suppose there is a finite set $A\subset\mathfrak h^\vee$ such that $$\{\mu:M_\mu\ne0\}\subseteq\bigcup_{\eta\in A}(\eta-\mathbf Z_{\ge0}\Delta).$$ Assume that each of the operators $e_i$ and $f_i$ is locally nilpotent on $M$, meaning that for every $v\in M$ some positive power of that operator kills $v$. Then only finitely many $M_\mu$ are nonzero, and $M$ is finite-dimensional over $\mathbf Q$. Empty $A$ and the zero Lie algebra are allowed.

source.place: Section 23h, printed p.508 (weight gradation) and p.511, proof of Corollary 23.73 (highest-weight background). WANTED: Serre, Complex Semisimple Lie Algebras, Chapter VII, finite-dimensionality argument for integrable highest-weight quotients. The stated general weight-module criterion is the agent formulation of that argument; it assumes no finite-dimensional ambient module.

proof.text: If $A=\varnothing$, the support is empty, so the assumed direct-sum decomposition gives $M=0$. If $r=0$, the simple-root basis in the hypotheses is empty, hence $\mathfrak h^\vee=0$; there is at most the weight $0$, and $M=M_0$ is finite-dimensional by hypothesis. Henceforth assume $A\ne\varnothing$ and $r>0$.

source.place: Agent argument for the general criterion supporting Section 23h, printed pp.508 and 511; the general infinite-dimensional criterion is not asserted in Milne.

proof.text: Write $xv$ for the given action. On $L=\mathfrak g\oplus M$ put $[(x,u),(y,v)]=([x,y],xv-yu)$, and identify $\mathfrak h$ with $\mathfrak h\oplus0$. This is a Lie algebra by [def-wf-lie-algebra]: the bracket is bilinear and alternating; for three pairs $(x,u),(y,v),(z,w)$, its Jacobi identity has first component the Jacobi identity of $\mathfrak g$ and second component the cyclic sum of $x(yw)-y(xw)-[x,y]w$, which vanishes by the representation identity. Thus $0\oplus M$ is an abelian ideal and $[(h,0),(0,v)]=(0,hv)$.

source.place: Agent argument for the general criterion supporting Section 23h, printed pp.508 and 511; the general infinite-dimensional criterion is not asserted in Milne.

proof.text: Fix $i$ and put $E_i=(e_i,0)$, $F_i=(f_i,0)$, $H_i=(h_{\alpha_i},0)$. The normalized triples and root brackets of [lem-sfb-split-semisimple-root-decomposition] give all the bracket hypotheses of [lem-sfb-integrable-sl2-reflection-automorphism]. On $L$, $\operatorname{ad}E_i$ is the direct sum of $\operatorname{ad}e_i$ on $\mathfrak g$ and $e_i$ on $M$; the first is nilpotent by the root-decomposition node and the second locally nilpotent by hypothesis. Taking the larger of the two annihilating exponents proves local nilpotence on each pair. The same holds for $F_i$. Apply the cited reflection theorem with $\mathfrak t=\mathfrak h\oplus0$ and $\alpha=\alpha_i$. Each exponential and its inverse preserves $0\oplus M$, since every power of its defining adjoint operator does; consequently their product restricts to an invertible linear map on $M$. Intersecting the weight-space isomorphism in the reflection theorem with this invariant ideal gives $M_\mu\simeq M_{s_i\mu}$, where $s_i\mu=\mu-\mu(h_{\alpha_i})\alpha_i$. In particular $M_\mu\ne0$ if and only if $M_{s_i\mu}\ne0$.

source.place: Agent argument for the general criterion supporting Section 23h, printed pp.508 and 511; the general infinite-dimensional criterion is not asserted in Milne.

proof.text:
Let $W$ be the subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak h^\vee)$ generated by these simple reflections. It is a subgroup of the finite group generated by all root reflections in [lem-sfb-split-semisimple-root-decomposition], so it is finite; put $d=|W|\ge1$. Step 3 shows that $w\mu$ is a weight for every weight $\mu$ and every $w\in W$: apply its equivalence successively along a word in the generators, whose inverses equal themselves. Define the rational linear functional $\ell$ by $\ell(\alpha_i)=1$ on the simple-root basis. Put $C=\max(\{0\}\cup\{\ell(\eta):\eta\in A\})$. The upper-cone hypothesis implies $\ell(
u)\le C$ for every weight $
u$, because $
u=\eta-\sum_i n_i\alpha_i$ with $n_i\ge0$ gives $\ell(
u)=\ell(\eta)-\sum_i n_i$.

source.place: Agent argument for the general criterion supporting Section 23h, printed pp.508 and 511; the general infinite-dimensional criterion is not asserted in Milne.

proof.text: The linear functional $B(x)=\sum_{w\in W}\ell(wx)$ is invariant under each $s_i$, since $w\mapsto ws_i$ permutes $W$. As $\alpha_i(h_{\alpha_i})=2$, we have $s_i\alpha_i=-\alpha_i$; hence $B(\alpha_i)=B(-\alpha_i)=-B(\alpha_i)$ and $B(\alpha_i)=0$ over $\mathbf Q$. The $\alpha_i$ are a basis, so $B=0$. For a weight $\mu$, every $w\mu$ is a weight, and therefore $0=\sum_w\ell(w\mu)\le\ell(\mu)+(d-1)C$. Thus $\ell(\mu)\ge-(d-1)C$.

source.place: Agent argument for the general criterion supporting Section 23h, printed pp.508 and 511; the general infinite-dimensional criterion is not asserted in Milne.

proof.text: For every weight choose a presentation $\mu=\eta-\sum_i n_i\alpha_i$ with $\eta\in A$ and $n_i\in\mathbf Z_{\ge0}$. The preceding inequality gives $\sum_i n_i=\ell(\eta)-\ell(\mu)\le\ell(\eta)+(d-1)C\le dC$. Choose an integer $N\ge dC$. Every $n_i$ belongs to the finite set $\{0,\ldots,N\}$. Hence the support is contained in the image of the finite set $A\times\{0,\ldots,N\}^r$ under $(\eta,(n_i))\mapsto\eta-\sum_i n_i\alpha_i$. It is finite. This uses the integral, rather than merely real, cone in the hypothesis.

source.place: Agent argument for the general criterion supporting Section 23h, printed pp.508 and 511; the general infinite-dimensional criterion is not asserted in Milne.

proof.text: Take a finite basis of each nonzero $M_\mu$. There are only finitely many such spaces by step 6, so the union of these bases is finite. It spans $M$ by the assumed ordinary direct-sum decomposition. Thus $M$ is finite-dimensional over $\mathbf Q$, and both conclusions follow.
